screens.body:
'The cloud' is just someone else's computer — one you rent by the minute instead of buying. When your app runs 'in the cloud,' it runs on servers in a giant data center owned by Amazon, Google, or Microsoft.

You get the power without the hardware. No buying servers, no server room, no 2 AM drive to reboot a machine.

options: Renting compute by the minute on someone else's servers
Storing files only on your laptop
check.question: The cloud is…

screens.heading: The cloud in one sentence

screens.body:
Renting beats owning for three reasons: scale (handle 10 users or 10 million without rewiring), no upfront hardware cost, and pay-as-you-go (quiet month = small bill).

That's why startups and side projects live in the cloud. SwiftGigs' database on Supabase? That's cloud — you never touched a physical server.

options: It looks impressive on a resume
Scale on demand, no hardware, pay for what you use
check.question: Why rent instead of own?

screens.heading: Why rent?

screens.body:
A container is a sealed box holding your app plus everything it needs to run: the language runtime, libraries, settings. If it runs on your laptop in the box, it runs identically on any server.

Docker is the standard tool for building these boxes. 'It works on my machine' stops being a joke because the box IS the machine.

options: Your app plus all its dependencies, sealed in a box
check.question: A container is…

screens.heading: Containers: ship the whole box
screens.keyPoint: Same box everywhere = no 'works on my machine'.

screens.body:
A virtual machine (VM) pretends to be an entire computer, operating system included — heavy, slow to start, each one gigabytes. A container shares the host's OS and only packages your app — light, starts in seconds, megabytes.

Rule of thumb: VMs isolate whole systems; containers package single apps. Most modern deploys use containers.

options: VMs virtualize a whole OS (heavy); containers share the OS (light)
check.question: Containers vs VMs:

screens.heading: Containers vs VMs
screens.keyPoint: VMs = whole fake computers. Containers = light app boxes.

screens.body:
Serverless takes it further: you write a single function ('when a file uploads, make a thumbnail'), and the cloud runs it only when triggered. No server to manage at all — not even a container.

You pay per run, down to fractions of a cent. Perfect for spiky workloads; wasteful if the function runs nonstop.

options: Code that runs on triggers, no server to manage, pay per run
check.question: Serverless means…

screens.heading: Serverless: no server at all
screens.keyPoint: Write a function, pay per run, manage nothing.

screens.body:
You already deployed to the cloud: Learn SD went to Vercel. You pushed code, Vercel built it and served it worldwide — no server config, no SSH, no nginx.

That's the modern flow: git push → cloud builds → live URL. Platforms like Vercel, Netlify, and Render turned deployment from a weekend project into a button.

options: Git push → the platform builds and hosts it
You emailed your code to Vercel
check.question: How did Learn SD get on Vercel?

screens.heading: Your first cloud deploy
screens.keyPoint: Push code, get a live URL. You've done this.

screens.body:
The cloud isn't magic — it's trade-offs. Bills can surprise you (always set alerts), you're renting so the provider sets the rules (lock-in), and debugging a distributed system is harder than one laptop.

Smart devs learn the pricing page before the feature list. Free tiers are generous; runaway bills are not a myth.

options: Set billing alerts and learn pricing first
check.question: The #1 cloud rookie mistake to avoid:

screens.heading: The trade-offs
screens.keyPoint: Great power, real bills. Alerts on, pricing read.
